uses: In folk practice the dark, cooked berries of the elder are made into syrups and thick fruit robs taken through the cold and flu season. Homemade elderberry wine was warmed and sipped as a winter cordial. The berries are also cooked into jams, jellies and chutneys. The elder tree itself holds a large place in European folklore.
taste: Fruity with a sharp tang once cooked
caution_pregnancy: Little is known about whether elderberry is safe for health purposes during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Not enough is known; avoid medicinal amounts.
caution_medications: No specific interactions are listed in the sources we used, but NCCIH advises talking with a health care provider before combining elderberry with any medicine, since some herbs and medicines interact harmfully.
caution_conditions: Raw or unripe berries contain substances that can release cyanide and cause nausea, vomiting and severe diarrhea; large amounts can make you seriously ill. Always cook the berries, and pick out every stem. The leaves, stems, roots and seeds are listed as poisonous too, and the bark is a strong purgative. There is no good evidence elderberry helps with COVID-19, so don't rely on it for that. In one small study of people with autoimmune skin diseases (dermatomyositis and skin lupus), flare-ups often followed elderberry use; the study couldn't show that elderberry caused them. If you have an autoimmune condition or take medicine that damps down the immune system, talk with your doctor first.
caution_duration: Not enough is known; none of our sources sets a safe length of use.
caution_topical: Not enough is known about using elderberry preparations on the skin.
garden_harvest_timing: Cut whole clusters when every berry is fully ripe and black, late summer into fall; strip berries from the stems before cooking.
garden_sun: Full sun to part shade; fruits best in full sun
garden_water: Moist, rich soil with good drainage
notes: A fast-growing shrub or small tree that suckers and self-seeds and can turn weedy. Birds love the fruit; plant more than one variety for a better crop. Grieve records the belief that an Elder Mother lived in the tree and that leave was asked before cutting it, and that elder leaves hung at doors kept witches out. The EMA could not write a monograph for elderberry because traditional-use data were incomplete.
